subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Fast Radio Bursts
description: A quick, practical guide to Fast Radio Bursts.

hook.text: Fast radio bursts are millisecond flashes of radio waves from billions of light-years away. Nobody knows exactly what causes them.

buildup.text: The first was found in 2007 by Duncan Lorimer in archival data. Hundreds have been detected since, mostly one-time events.

discovery.text: In 2020, a magnetar in the Milky Way produced an FRB-like burst—the first time a source was identified for these signals.

twist.text: Some FRBs repeat. FRB 20121102A fires hundreds of bursts, suggesting its source survives each explosion.

climax.text: CHIME telescope in Canada detects multiple FRBs daily. The mystery is shrinking, but surprises keep coming.

punchline.text: Millisecond flashes from billions of light-years away. Magnetars are the prime suspect.

quiz.question: What is the leading candidate for the source of fast radio bursts?
options: Magnetars—neutron stars with extremely powerful magnetic fields
Colliding black holes at the centers of distant galaxies
Alien civilizations sending interstellar communication signals

details.summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are intense millisecond-long flashes of radio waves from billions of light-years away. First detected in 2007, their origin was mysterious until 2020 when a magnetar in our galaxy produced one — linking at least some FRBs to highly magnetized neutron stars.
details.whyItMatters: FRBs are a frontier of modern astrophysics — thousands occur daily across the sky. They probe the material between galaxies and could become powerful cosmological tools for mapping the universe's hidden matter.
takeaways: Intense millisecond radio flashes from billions of light-years away
At least some originate from magnetars
Thousands occur across the sky every day

faq.question: What makes FRBs so energetic despite being brief?
faq.answer: In a single millisecond, an FRB releases as much energy as the Sun does in three days — but concentrated entirely in radio wavelengths and a narrow beam. The emission mechanism likely involves the extreme magnetic fields of magnetars, which can exceed 10^15 gauss.

faq.question: Why are FRBs useful for cosmology?
faq.answer: Radio waves from FRBs are dispersed by free electrons between galaxies. Measuring this dispersion reveals the amount of intervening matter. FRBs may solve the 'missing baryon problem' — accounting for the ordinary matter predicted to exist but not detected in galaxies.
